newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - EU Commission to ban Clabecq aid.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - EU Commission to ban Clabecq aid.

text.p: The European Commission is expected to rule next week that a 1.5-billion-Belgian-franc ($47 million) capital injection for steel maker Forges de Clabecq amounts to an inadmissable public subsidy.

A Commission official said a draft decision concluded "unequivocally" that the capital injection by the Belgian region of Wallonia and other rescue measures represented state aid -- something the Belgian authorities have strongly contested.
A definitive ruling is due in principle on December 18.

The European Coal and Steel Community (ECSC), one of the European Union's founding bodies, bans subsidies to the steel industry in general. Restructuring and other forms of aid can still be allowed by EU industry ministers acting unanimously.
Belgium has always contested that the Clabecq plan involved subsidies, arguing instead that Wallonia was acting within its right as the main shareholder of Clabecq.

"They have asked us to confirm that the plan did not involve state aid," the Commission official said. The Commission had no choice but to say: "this amounts to subsidies and subsidies are prohibited under the ECSC treaty".
It is all the more difficult for the Belgian authorities to have their way now, given that Clabecq is one of the last companies to be restructured in the Union.
EU ministers approved in 1994 subsidies to help restructure six loss-making firms in Italy, Germany, Spain and Portugal. The companies concerned include Italy's Ilva SpA.
"They will say we are being tougher with Clabecq than with Ilva, but they are the ones to blame," another source said.
Walloon leader Robert Collignon told RTBF television industrially run-down Wallonia would fight for the survival of Clabecq and jobs at the company and sub-contractors.
"I continue to defend with conviction a case which is without doubt a special one," he said.

"If the Commission maintains this opinion...it's clear that we will continue to the very end of the process; that is to say, beyond the opinion of the Commission there is always the process before the Council of Ministers," Collignon added.
Roberto Dorazzio, trade union leader at Clabecq, said a negative decision from the European Commission would lead to 1,700 direct redundancies and 3,500 indirect job losses.
Workers planned to demonstrate outside the European Parliament building in Brussels, he added.
Belgium has not said whether it will re-submit the rescue plan under article 95 of the ESCS treaty, the sources said.
The Commission is still closely monitoring the restructuring of the six European steel makers aided in 1994 to avoid the European steel sector plunging back into an overcapacity crisis.

Analysts said that after the Commission's decision, the outlook for Clabecq was grim. "I'm afraid this will be the end for Clabecq, I don't see any other thing that could help the firm now," said Patrik Geldermans at Kredietbank.

On the Brussels bourse there were only indicative prices for Clabecq shares on Monday. Due to a large number of sellers, the bourse said, the stock would be marked down by 10 percent at Tuesday's opening. Friday's close was 175 francs. ($1=31.69 Belgian Franc)
